Option B says a smaller sample, n = 25, has fewer chances for error. That is the defect: it treats sample size as a source of error. A smaller n increases the standard error of p̂, which makes detecting the true difference harder and lowers power.

You picked B, which gives a standard deviation of −10. The mean of 74 is correct, but the spread is not. A standard deviation can never be negative, so this choice fails the requirement that the spread be a valid measure of variability.

Choice B gives the right mean, 74, but a standard deviation of −10. That is the error. A standard deviation measures spread and cannot be negative. The multiplier −4 changes the sign of the scores, but the spread uses its absolute value: 4(2.5) = 10.

How the point is lost: the answer is wrong on the standard deviation alone. Next time, take the absolute value of the multiplier before scaling the standard deviation, and state the result as a nonnegative number. This is a "learn this first" fix: for y = a + bx, the mean is a + b·x̄, and the standard deviation is |b|·s_x. Adding a constant changes the mean but not the standard deviation.

subject: ap-statistics
text:
What the question requires: explain why two random samples from one school give different percentages, using the idea that a sample value changes from sample to sample while the school's true value does not.
